steps.title: Two kinds of work: talk, then think
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.1 · STEP 1 OF 14
Two kinds of work: talk, then think

Every block does two things in order. Attention lets the words share information. Then each word, on its own, works with what it now knows. Switch between them.

WHAT IT IS

A block is one round of attention (words exchange information) followed by an MLP (each word processes what it now has). You met attention in Lesson 1; the next two steps open up the MLP, then the residual stream.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A team meeting, then desk work. In the meeting everyone shares what they know (attention). Then each person goes back to their desk and works through it alone, using their own expertise (MLP).
Technical
A JOIN, then a MAP. Attention is like a join: each row looks at the other rows. The MLP is like rows.map(f): the same function applied to every row independently, with no row seeing another.
Attention: words talk
MLP: each word thinks alone
Replay ▶
value dots from earlier words flow into bank
The
river
bank

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Attention is the only place where words see each other. The MLP uses the same weights for every word and runs on all of them in parallel, which is why it's cheap to batch on a GPU.

EVIDENCE

The original transformer paper describes every layer this way: “Each layer has two sub-layers”, multi-head self-attention and “a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network” (the MLP), which is “applied to each position separately and identically” (sections 3.1 and 3.3). Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017) ↗

Go deeper

A model repeats this block dozens of times. Attention and the MLP alternate, always in this order.

steps.title: One neuron is one yes/no question
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.1 · STEP 2 OF 14
One neuron is one yes/no question

A neuron checks the word for one pattern and answers with a number: positive means yes, zero means no. Flip the two facts and see when this one says yes.

WHAT IT IS

A neuron (originally called a perceptron, hence the P in MLP) does three things: a dot product of the word's vector with its learned weights (Basics, step 11), plus a bias, then it keeps the result only if it's positive (ReLU = max(0, x)).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A safe-deposit box that needs two keys. One key alone does nothing; both together open it. The bias decides how many keys it takes.
Technical
One rule in a rules engine: if (nearRiver && isBank) → emit signal. Except nobody writes the rule: training learns the weights and bias.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

The word's vector has thousands of numbers, and “river earlier” or “is bank” are directions in it, not literal yes/no inputs. The dot product measures how strongly the vector points that way; the bias and ReLU turn that into “fires” or “silent”.

EVIDENCE

3Blue1Brown builds the same neuron for a fact: weights pointing at “Michael” + “Jordan” with a bias of −1, so it fires only for the full name, and then adds “basketball”. How might LLMs store facts ↗

Go deeper

The bias (−1) is a threshold: one fact alone scores 0, so the neuron stays silent; both together score 1. Real neurons check fuzzy patterns, not exact facts, but the shape is the same.

steps.title: The MLP: thousands of questions, then add the answers
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.1 · STEP 3 OF 14
The MLP: thousands of questions, then add the answers

The MLP asks the word thousands of questions at once, keeps the yes answers, and turns each yes into a note added back to the word. Press Run, then switch the sentence.

WHAT IT IS

MLP = multi-layer perceptron: a small neural network with two layers of neurons, applied to each word separately. Layer 1 asks thousands of yes/no-style questions about the word (widen). Layer 2 turns the yes answers into notes and adds them back to the word's vector (narrow).

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A doctor's intake checklist. Hundreds of questions (fever? cough? recent travel?). Each yes adds a line to the chart (“possible flu”). The chart grows; nothing on it is erased.
Technical
A fraud rules engine. Thousands of rules check each transaction on its own; every rule that matches attaches a signal to it. Downstream systems read the signals, not the raw rules.
The river bank…
Cash at the bank…
Run the MLP ▶

Brightness = how strongly a neuron fires (0.5 glows half as bright as 1.0). Blue lines = positive weights. Each question also has a bias (−1 or −0.5) that sets its threshold. Switch “run on”: the same weights, run on each word separately, write different notes.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

In numbers: notes = W_down · max(0, W_up · x + b), then x = x + notes. W_up holds the questions (one row per neuron), W_down holds the note each neuron writes. Both are learned weights, frozen at inference (when the model is used, not trained).

EVIDENCE

MLPs are most of a model: in GPT-3 they hold about 116 billion of its 175 billion parameters (roughly two-thirds), and they're where factual associations like “Jordan → basketball” are thought to live. Real neurons are messier than these five: features are spread across many neurons (“superposition”). 3Blue1Brown, How might LLMs store facts ↗

Go deeper

Real MLPs ask about 3.5–4× as many questions as the vector has numbers (e.g. 14,336 for 4,096 in Llama 3 8B), then fold the answers back into 4,096. The activation is often a smooth cousin of ReLU (GELU or SwiGLU).

steps.title: The residual stream: a notepad every layer adds to
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.1 · STEP 4 OF 14
The residual stream: a notepad every layer adds to

Each word carries one vector through the whole model, its notepad. Every attention and MLP step reads it and adds a note; nothing is lost by default. Run the layers, then try overwriting.

WHAT IT IS

The residual stream is the word's vector as it travels through the model. “Residual” means each layer's output is added to what was already there (a “residual connection”), instead of replacing it.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A shared document passed down a line of reviewers. Each one reads it and adds comments in the margin. Nobody deletes anything by default (a reviewer can only write a correction), so the last reviewer sees every earlier comment, and the original text.
Technical
Middleware on a request: every handler reads the request context and attaches fields (ctx.user, ctx.locale), instead of building a new request and dropping the old fields.

Always the same size: 4,096 numbers. A note is a nudge in a direction, not a new line. Layers can write negative nudges that cancel earlier notes (watch cell 2, numbered above the strip: block 1's attention adds +0.3, block 2's MLP takes it back), but nothing is lost by default.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

In numbers: x = x + attention(x), then x = x + MLP(x), in every block. Because of the additions, the final vector is literally the original embedding plus every layer's contribution. It also lets training nudges flow straight back to early layers.

EVIDENCE

Anthropic's interpretability work describes the residual stream as a communication channel: every layer reads from it with a projection and writes back by adding, so the stream is the sum of all previous layers' outputs plus the original embedding. Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (2021) ↗

Go deeper

Before each read, the vector is rescaled (normalization) so the numbers stay in a sane range as notes pile up.

steps.title: Stack the blocks: each block sharpens the guess
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.1 · STEP 5 OF 14
Stack the blocks: each block sharpens the guess

A model stacks the same kind of block many times, each with its own weights. Every block adds notes the next one can build on, so the guess for the next word gets sharper with depth. Drag the depth.

WHAT IT IS

A transformer = embedding → N blocks (each: attention + MLP on the residual stream) → scoring every word. Common 7–8B models use 32 blocks. The blocks have the same shape but different weights, so each learns a different job.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Editing a draft in passes. The first pass fixes spelling, the next grammar, then meaning, then the ending. Each pass works on the previous pass's result, which is why order and depth matter.
Technical
A compiler's optimization passes over the same intermediate representation: each pass rewrites it a little, and later passes rely on what earlier ones did.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Depth is what lets the model chain steps: block 3 can use a note block 2 wrote (“it's a riverside”) to add a new one (“floods are likely”). One block can only do one round of talk-then-think. Every block has its own weights, so depth costs memory: the classic GPT formula is about 12 × width² parameters per block (4 × width² for attention, 8 × width² for the MLP): 12 × 4,096² × 32 blocks ≈ 6.4B parameters ≈ 12.9 GB at 16-bit. Newer models differ: Llama 3 8B has a gated MLP (three matrices of 4,096 × 14,336 instead of two) and smaller key and value weights, because several heads share one set of keys and values (2.3 shows how), so a block is about 218M parameters; 32 blocks ≈ 7.0B, plus 1.05B for the input and output word tables ≈ 8.0B.

EVIDENCE

The logit lens: apply the model's final scoring step to the residual stream after each block, and you can read its next-word guess at every depth. Early blocks guess vaguely; the right word rises as blocks accumulate. nostalgebraist, interpreting GPT: the logit lens (2020) ↗

Go deeper

The percentages here are illustrative, shaped like what researchers see when they read a real model's guess after each block.

steps.title: The last vector scores every token in the vocabulary
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.2 · STEP 6 OF 14
The last vector scores every token in the vocabulary

After the last block, the final vector is compared with a row for every vocabulary token (a dot product). Those scores are the logits; softmax turns them into probabilities. Switch the context.

WHAT IT IS

Logits are raw scores, one for every word in the vocabulary (about 100,000), made by comparing bank's final vector with each word's row in the unembedding table. Softmax (Basics, step 12) turns them into probabilities that add up to 100%. This answers the lesson's question.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Scoring one job posting against every applicant's CV: one match score per applicant, then turned into shortlist chances.
Technical
Brute-force ranking with no index: score every candidate against the query on every request, then normalize the scores into a distribution.
The river bank…

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

logits = W_unembed · x, a vocabulary × width table (100k × 4,096 ≈ 410 million multiply-adds per generated token for this step alone). It's the same shape as the embedding table; some models share the two.

EVIDENCE

Researchers reuse exactly this scoring step on the middle of the model to read its guess after each block (the logit lens from 2.1, step 5). interpreting GPT: the logit lens ↗

Go deeper

The table of rows is the unembedding matrix: one row per vocabulary token, the same shape as the embedding table (some models share the two). Real models score about 100k tokens at every step. Backend version: brute-force ranking of every candidate on every request, then turning scores into shares.

steps.title: Temperature: how sharp the choice is
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.2 · STEP 7 OF 14
Temperature: how sharp the choice is

Before softmax, the logits are divided by the temperature. Low temperature sharpens toward the top token, high temperature flattens. Drag it.

WHAT IT IS

Temperature is a number set per request (the temperature parameter in an API call). The logits are divided by it before softmax.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A strict judge versus a relaxed one. Strict (low temperature): the favorite almost always wins. Relaxed (high): underdogs get real chances.
Technical
A sharpness knob on weighted routing: low sends nearly all traffic to the best backend, high spreads it across many.

logits ÷ 1.00 = [5.44, 3.84, 1.72, 0.67, 2.40] → softmax

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

p = softmax(logits / T). As T → 0 you get greedy decoding (always the top word). T = 1 is the model's own distribution. T > 1 flattens it. Dividing by a small number stretches the gaps, and softmax's exponent turns stretched gaps into a near-certain winner.

EVIDENCE

The decoding rule matters as much as the model: “decoding strategies alone can dramatically effect the quality” of generated text, and always taking the most likely word (the T → 0 end of this slider) gives text that is “bland and strangely repetitive”. Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (ICLR 2020) ↗

Go deeper

Dividing by a small number stretches the gaps between logits, and softmax's exponent turns stretched gaps into a near-certain winner. As temperature approaches 0 you get greedy decoding: always the top token. Even at temperature 0, a served model can occasionally differ between runs, because tiny floating-point differences change when requests are batched differently.

steps.title: Sampling: roll the dice, but cut the tail
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.2 · STEP 8 OF 14
Sampling: roll the dice, but cut the tail

The next token is drawn at random by these probabilities. Top-p keeps only the most likely tokens that together reach p, so unlikely ones can't be picked. Sample 50 times.

WHAT IT IS

Sampling means drawing the next word at random according to its probability. Top-p (also called nucleus sampling) first keeps only the most likely words whose probabilities add up to p, then draws among them.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Picking tonight's restaurant by rolling dice, but only among the places that make up 90% of your past visits, never the one you tried once and hated.
Technical
Weighted random load balancing that first drops every backend below a cumulative-weight cutoff, then picks among the rest.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Sort words by probability, keep the smallest set reaching p (e.g. 0.9), rescale them to 100%, draw one. Top-k is the blunter version: keep the k best. A long answer is hundreds of these draws, so one unlucky pick can steer everything after it.

EVIDENCE

Always picking the most likely word makes text “bland and strangely repetitive”; nucleus sampling keeps variety while cutting the unreliable tail. Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (ICLR 2020) ↗

Go deeper

Top-k is the blunter cousin: keep the k best tokens. Sampling happens once per token, so a long answer is hundreds of dice rolls, and one unlucky pick can steer everything after it. Backend version: weighted random load balancing that drops low-weight backends before choosing.

steps.title: Generation is a loop: one token per pass
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 9 OF 14
Generation is a loop: one token per pass

The model only ever predicts one next token. To write more, it appends that token and runs again. Press Generate 1 token and watch how much work each pass repeats; then turn the cache on.

WHAT IT IS

Autoregressive generation: the model predicts one token, appends it to the input, and runs the whole model again, until it emits a stop token or hits a length limit. Our answer, “flooded”, was pass 1.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Tapping your phone's autocomplete over and over: each tap adds one word, and the next suggestion depends on everything typed so far.
Technical
A loop whose output feeds its next input, like a fold over time, rather than one batch call that returns the whole answer.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Each pass runs every block on the sequence. Earlier tokens never change (a token only looks backward), so the keys and values computed for them on earlier passes are still valid. The next steps exploit that.

EVIDENCE

The original transformer paper states the loop directly: “At each step the model is auto-regressive, consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next” (section 3). Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (2017) ↗

Go deeper

Each pass runs the whole stack of blocks. Without reuse, pass k reprocesses the prompt and every token generated so far, even though their keys and values haven't changed (a token only looks backward, so later tokens can't change earlier ones). The next steps show what gets reused.

steps.title: Without a cache, work grows with the square of the length
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 10 OF 14
Without a cache, work grows with the square of the length

Recomputing every earlier token on every pass adds up fast. Move the prompt and output lengths and compare.

WHAT IT IS

Without reuse, pass k reprocesses the whole prompt plus the k − 1 tokens already generated, even though nothing about them changed.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Rereading a whole book from page one every time you want to write the next sentence of your review.
Technical
Recomputing an aggregate from scratch on every request instead of maintaining it incrementally, like a materialized view.
prompt tokens: 100
output tokens: 2000

← passes

teal = new work (with a cache, only this)

cache entries read with a cache: n·prompt + n²/2. The red area doesn't vanish; it becomes reads.

Why the two big numbers aren't a wash: a read fetches one stored key and value; a recompute runs a token through every layer's projections and MLP: far more math per position.

The cache removes the repeated projection and MLP work. Attention still reads every cached key and value on every step, so each new token costs a little more than the last.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

For n output tokens: about n × prompt + n²/2 token positions without a cache, versus prompt + n with one. At 2,000 output tokens after a 100-token prompt that's about 2.2 million versus 2,100.

EVIDENCE

Even with a cache, the reads are the bottleneck: one-token-at-a-time decoding is “often slow, due to the memory-bandwidth cost of repeatedly loading the large” key and value tensors. That paper's fix, sharing keys and values across heads, is the ancestor of grouped-query attention (GQA), coming up in “How big is the KV cache?”. Shazeer, Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (2019) ↗

Go deeper

Without a cache: output token k reprocesses the prompt plus k earlier outputs, so the total is n × prompt + n²/2. With a cache, each token is processed once: prompt + n. Backend version: recomputing a running total from scratch on every request versus keeping the running total.

steps.title: The KV cache: compute keys and values once, keep them
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 11 OF 14
The KV cache: compute keys and values once, keep them

Earlier tokens' keys and values never change, so the model stores them. Each new token computes only its own query, key and value, then reads the rest from the cache. Step through.

WHAT IT IS

The KV cache stores every earlier token's key and value vectors (from attention, Lesson 1) for every layer, so later passes read them instead of recomputing them. K and V are the two things a token offers to others; the query is only needed for the newest token.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Taking notes as you read, so you never reread a page: each new page is read once and added to the notes.
Technical
Memoization keyed by position: compute (k_i, v_i) once, append to a per-request store, read it on every later step.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Each decode step computes q, k, v for the new token only, appends its k and v, then attends over the whole cache. The cache grows by one row per token per layer and lives in GPU memory for the whole request.

EVIDENCE

The cache is large and grows during a request; naive management wastes memory through fragmentation and duplication, which caps batch size. vLLM's PagedAttention manages it like OS virtual-memory pages: near-zero waste and 2–4× throughput at the same latency versus FasterTransformer and Orca. Kwon et al., PagedAttention (SOSP 2023) ↗

Go deeper

Queries aren't cached: only the newest token asks a question each step. The cache grows by one row per token, per layer, and lives in GPU memory for as long as the request runs. So each decode step does little math but reads a lot of memory: all the weights plus the whole cache, to produce one token. That's why decode is limited by memory bandwidth. Backend version: write-once memoization keyed by position, in an append-only store.

steps.title: Prefill and decode are two different jobs
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 12 OF 14
Prefill and decode are two different jobs

The prompt is processed in one parallel pass (prefill), which sets the time to first token. Then tokens come out one at a time (decode), each tick reading all the weights. Batch users, then try 8-bit weights.

WHAT IT IS

Prefill: process the whole prompt in one parallel pass and fill the cache; it sets TTFT (time to first token). Decode: produce tokens one at a time; it sets TPOT (time per output token). Compute-bound means the GPU's math units are the limit; memory-bound (memory-bandwidth-bound) means the limit is how fast bytes arrive from memory, and the math units wait. Prefill is compute-bound, decode memory-bound.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A kitchen's prep and service. Prep chops everything at once before the first plate goes out; service then sends plates one by one.
Technical
A bulk load versus point queries: prefill is one big parallel batch (compute-bound); decode is many tiny sequential reads of all the weights and the cache (memory-bandwidth-bound).

One user: every 21.1 ms tick reads all 140.0 GB of weights to make one token, and the GPU's math sits nearly idle. Try “max that fits”.

Batching shares each read of the weights; KV memory caps the batch. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave at every step.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Decode does little math per byte it reads, so a GPU serving one request mostly waits on memory. Batching many users' decode ticks together shares each read of the weights, and KV memory per request caps how many fit, which is why it decides throughput. Continuous batching schedules per tick: requests join and leave the batch at every step.

EVIDENCE

Orca found that with per-batch scheduling “newly arrived requests have to wait until the current batch completely finishes”. Its fix, “iteration-level scheduling”, runs “only a single iteration of the model on the batch” at a time, so requests join and leave between ticks; it reports up to 36.9× throughput over FasterTransformer at the same latency. Yu et al., Orca (OSDI 2022) ↗ Batching prefill and decode together causes “strong prefill-decoding interferences”; DistServe runs the two phases on different GPUs. Zhong et al., DistServe (OSDI 2024) ↗

Go deeper

Prefill is compute-bound: thousands of tokens' worth of math in parallel. Decode is memory-bound: one token per user per full read of the weights and caches. Plain batching runs many users' decode ticks together so they share each weight read. Continuous batching (Orca's iteration-level scheduling) goes further: requests join and leave the batch at every tick, so a finished request's slot is refilled at once instead of waiting for the whole batch. Interview metrics: TTFT (time to first token), TPOT or ITL (time per output token), and throughput (tokens per second across all users).

steps.title: How big is the KV cache?
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 13 OF 14
How big is the KV cache?

The KV cache, not the weights, often decides how many users fit on a GPU. Every layer stores a key and a value per KV head, for every token. Switch to GQA and watch it shrink.

WHAT IT IS

Per token, each layer stores one key and one value for each KV head. Grouped-query attention (GQA) lets several query heads share one KV head, which shrinks the cache.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
Luggage on a plane: the hold is fixed; the longer each passenger's trip (context), the more luggage, and the fewer passengers fit.
Technical
Session state per connection: a server's RAM caps concurrent sessions by per-session state size, not by CPU.
8B-class · 1 GPU
70B-class · 2 GPUs
KV heads: one per query head
KV heads: 8 (GQA)
64 query heads (one dot each)
8 key/value slots stored per layer per token (8 query heads share each)

Grouped-query attention (GQA), in plain words: query heads are split into groups, and each group shares one key/value head. The model still asks as many questions (queries), but stores far fewer keys and values per token.

16-bit cache
8-bit cache
context per request (tokens): 8,192

2 (K and V) × 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 328 KB per token

per request at 8,192 tokens

REAL SERVERS KEEP LESS FOR THE CACHE

vLLM's default gpu_memory_utilization is 0.92: it uses at most 92% of each GPU (the dashed line). At startup it also runs a test pass to measure peak activation memory (the scratch space a forward pass needs), and that comes out of the same budget. For 70B at 16-bit on 2 × 80 GB: 147.2 GB − 140 GB of weights = 7.2 GB, room for at most 2 of these 8K requests, fewer once activations are counted. So in practice teams shrink the weights (8-bit: 70 GB; 4-bit: 35 GB) or spread the model over more GPUs.

vLLM engine arguments ↗

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

bytes = 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes per number × tokens. A 70B-class model at 8K tokens is about 2.7 GB per request, so concurrency on a GPU is set by this number more than by the weights.

EVIDENCE

GQA uses a middle number of KV heads shared across groups of query heads and reaches quality close to full multi-head attention at speed close to multi-query attention. Ainslie et al., GQA (2023) ↗

Go deeper

Presets: an 8B-class model (32 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head size 128) on one 80 GB GPU, and a 70B-class model (80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head size 128) on two. Without GQA (64 KV heads) the 70B case would need 2.6 MB per token and 21.5 GB per 8K request: none fit. With GQA: about 328 KB per token and 2.7 GB per 8K-token request: about 7 fit beside the weights in theory, at most 2 under vLLM's default 92% cap. The levers are exactly the interview topics: fewer KV heads (grouped-query attention), an 8-bit cache (halves it; try the 8-bit switch), paged allocation so memory isn't wasted on fragments (PagedAttention, in vLLM), and sharing the cache for identical prompt prefixes (prefix caching).

steps.title: Why context windows have a limit
steps.text:
CHAPTER 2.3 · STEP 14 OF 14
Why context windows have a limit

Three costs grow with context: KV memory grows in line with it, attention work in prefill grows with its square, and the model only learned positions up to the length it was trained on. Drag the context.

WHAT IT IS

The context window is the maximum number of tokens (prompt + output) a model handles in one request.

THINK OF IT LIKE

Everyday
A desk: you can only spread out so many pages, a bigger desk takes more room, and scanning everything on it takes longer.
Technical
A bounded buffer whose memory grows linearly with size and whose full scan (attention in prefill) grows quadratically.
context length (tokens): 131,072
42.9 GB
KV cache for one request (70B-class, 16-bit)
8.59B
attention scores in prefill, per head per layer
2 × 80 GB = 160 GB
weights 140 GB + this request's cache
22.9 GB over capacity

Real 128K deployments use more GPUs, 8-bit weights or an 8-bit cache; this 2-GPU, 16-bit setup can't hold one 128K request (182.9 GB needed). The longest single request it can hold: 61,035 tokens using every byte, 21,972 under vLLM's 92% cap.

1M tokens of 70B-class cache ≈ 343.6 GB: more than both GPUs together, before the 140 GB of weights.

trained length (example: 131,072)
untrained positions
131,072

WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENING

Three limits: KV memory grows in line with tokens, prefill attention grows with their square, and the model only learned positions up to its training length. Long-context models extend training and cut costs (GQA, efficient attention kernels), but a 1M-token request still costs far more than a short one.

EVIDENCE

Position limits are real: models using rotary position embeddings “fail to generalize past the sequence length they were trained on”; YaRN extends the window with about 10× fewer tokens and 2.5× fewer training steps than earlier methods. Peng et al., YaRN (2023) ↗ And fitting a long context isn't the same as using it: accuracy is highest when the relevant text is at the start or end and drops in the middle, even for long-context models. Liu et al., Lost in the Middle (2023) ↗

Go deeper

Long-context models extend the trained range (RoPE scaling and long-context training) and cut the costs (grouped-query attention, smarter attention kernels), but memory and compute still grow with length. That's why serving systems cap context per tier, and why a 1M-token request costs far more than a short one. This is the bridge to 3.3, inference economics.
